article_text:
A coalition of Hollywood talent agencies and independent producers said Thursday that it supports the proposed U.S. tax incentive for film and TV production as a “first step,” but that more will need to be done to revive the industry.

The American Entertainment Alliance — which includes CAA , WME and UTA — is pushing for a revival of the fin-syn rules that allowed independent TV producers to thrive in the 1970s and ’80s.

But that goal risks complicating the campaign for a 20% federal incentive for domestic production, which has broader industry support and which advocates hope will pass by the end of the year.

The alliance — which also includes indie producers such as Blumhouse, Imagine Entertainment and MRC — emphasized that it is in “strong support” of the tax incentive, though it also said it will push for tweaks to make it more favorable for independents.

“This legislation is an urgent first step toward bringing production jobs home, and with targeted adjustments, it can also help level the playing field for independent producers,” the AEA said. “We will work closely with lawmakers and industry partners to strengthen the bill and shepherd the measure through the legislative process.”

The AEA announced its existence last week with a New York Times story in which agents and producers pushed for legislation to require streamers to buy 50% of their original content from independent production companies. The group argues that such legislation, which would also include time limits on exclusivity windows, is needed to restore competition and creativity in the TV business.

Though these ideas have been bandied about for the past year, they were not included in the federal tax credit bill introduced in Congress in September. In the statement, the coalition made clear that its goal is to pursue its legislation on a separate path in the next Congress.

“A tax credit alone will not restore a competitive American marketplace,” the group said. “That is why the AEA is advocating to restore a competitive American film and television market by pushing both for production incentives and a modern approach to creative ownership for the streaming era. We look forward to working with lawmakers and our counterparts in the 120th Congress to promote policies that expand opportunities for independent producers, strengthen competition, and let creators retain and reinvest the long-term value of their work.”

The federal incentive proposal includes a 5% bonus for independent productions. In the current bill language, an independent producer is defined as any company that is not publicly traded.

article_text:
Tom Skerritt , who starred in the TV series “Picket Fences” and appeared in movies ranging from “MASH” to “ Alien ,” “Top Gun,” “A River Runs Through It” and “Ted,” died on Wednesday of natural causes, Variety has confirmed with his publicist. He was 93.

The lean, rugged, mustachioed actor won an Emmy in 1993 and was also nominated in 1994 for playing Jimmy Brock, sheriff of the oddball town at the center of David E. Kelley’s CBS dramedy “Picket Fences.” He also shared SAG Award nominations for outstanding performance by an ensemble in a drama series for “Picket Fences” in 1995 and 1996 while also being nominated for outstanding performance by a male actor in a drama series in 1995.

Related Stories

In the 2000s he guested on “The West Wing” as a senator, on “Law & Order: SVU” as a biased judge and on HBO’s “Huff” as the father of Hank Azaria’s title character, replacing Robert Forster in the role. He recurred from 2006-09 on ABC’s “Brothers & Sisters” as family patriarch William Walker and guested on “The Good Wife” in 2014 and on “Madam Secretary” in 2015.

In Robert Altman’s “MASH” (1970), Skerritt played Duke Forrest, one of the insubordinate but excellent surgeons. The actor was third billed, after Donald Sutherland and Elliott Gould but before Sally Kellerman and Robert Duvall.

In Ridley’s classic sci-fi horror film ”Alien” (1979), Skerritt played Dallas, the captain of the Nostromo, and was first billed, ahead of Sigourney Weaver; he had originally turned down the part when the project had a low budget and no director attached. The actor also worked for Tony Scott, co-starring in the monumental 1986 hit “Top Gun” as Commander Mike “Viper” Metcalf, chief instructor at Miramar Naval Air Station’s so-called top gun school, where Tom Cruise’s Lieut. Pete “Maverick” Mitchell is training.

The Robert Redford-directed 1992 adaptation of Norman Maclean’s much-admired 1976 novella ”A River Runs Through It” afforded Skerritt with a relatively rare opportunity to do some serious acting in a film. He played a Presbyterian minister who is father to the characters played by Brad Pitt and Craig Sheffer, with the family only really united when they go fly fishing. Variety said: “Tom Skerritt discreetly reveals the loving core inside the reedy exterior of the boys’ preacher father.”

Skerritt was among the celebrities who cameo’d as themselves in Seth MacFarlane’s scabrous 2012 comedy “Ted.” He appeared in supporting roles as an academic in the 2013 campus-set romantic comedy “At Middleton,” starring Vera Farmiga and Andy Garcia, and as Ulysses S. Grant in “Field of Lost Shoes” (2014).

The year after “MASH” he appeared uncredited in “Harold and Maude” as a motorcycle cop.

He worked with Altman again in 1974’s “Thieves Like Us,” starring Keith Carradine and Shelley Duvall, and also appeared that year as a bank robber in Roger Corman cult classic “Big Bad Mama,” in which he was third billed after Angie Dickinson and William Shatner. Skerritt starred with Ernest Borgnine and Shatner in 1975 horror film “The Devil’s Rain.”

In Herbert Ross’ esteemed 1977 film “The Turning Point,” in which Anne Bancroft plays an aging dancer at New York’s Ballet Theater and Shirley MacLaine her old friend who moved to Oklahoma City and started a family, Skerritt played the MacLaine character’s husband, earning the National Board of Review’s best supporting actor award.

Skerritt also had a notable role in a very different vein in the 1978 Cheech and Chong movie “Up in Smoke,” in which he played Strawberry, the Cheech character’s cousin — a Vietnam vet who has a flashback during a police raid, believing the cops to be Viet Cong.

The actor had a sizable role in David Cronenberg’s 1983 adaptation of Stephen King’s “The Dead Zone.” Roger Ebert said: “The movie is filled with good performances [including] Tom Skerritt as the local sheriff who wants to enlist this psychic to solve a chain of murders.”

In 1988 he starred with Nancy Allen and Lara Flynn Boyle in “Poltergeist III.”

He played the father of Julia Roberts’ bride-t0-be in Herbert Ross’ “Steel Magnolias,” a 1989 hit movie that found little use for the men in the cast; the actor played the estranged father of Charlie Sheen’s character in Clint Eastwood’s “The Rookie” (1990). In the steamy 1992 thriller “Poison Ivy,” he played a father who’s all but ravished by the best friend of his daughter (Sara Gilbert): the evil, seductive Ivy, played by Drew Barrymore.

In the sixth season of the hit NBC sitcom “Cheers” (1987-88), Skerritt had a story arc as Evan Drake, boss to Kirstie Alley’s Rebecca Howe, who has an unrequited crush on him.

He starred as a small-town sheriff investigating a homicide in the well-regarded TV movie “The China Lake Murders” (1990).

After appearing in “Picket Fences” from 1992-96, he had a supporting role in Robert Zemeckis’ “Contact” (1997), starring Jodie Foster. The actor appeared in a series of TV movies and had supporting roles in “Texas Rangers” (2001) and Antoine Fuqua’s mercenary war drama “Tears of the Sun” (2003), starring Bruce Willis and Monica Bellucci. In 2010 he appeared in Mario Van Peebles’ “Redemption Road”; Variety said: “Tom Skerritt contributes a pitch-perfect supporting performance as the sage owner of a small-town honkytonk.”

Thomas Roy Skerritt was born in Detroit and attended Wayne State University and UCLA. He did a stint in the U.S. Air Force.

He made his feature debut in the Korean War drama “War Hunt” (1962), starring John Saxon and Sydney Pollack; Robert Redford had a small part, and Francis Ford Coppola had an uncredited role. He next appeared in the 1965 feature “Those Calloways.”

Skerritt made guest appearances on series including “The Alfred Hitchcock Hour,” “My Three Sons,” “Wagon Train,” “My Favorite Martian,” “The Fugitive” and “Gunsmoke” during the decade and on “Hawaii Five-O,” “Cannon,” “Barnaby Jones” and “Baretta” in the 1970s before his appearance in 1979’s “Alien” dialed up his career.

Skerritt was thrice married, the first time to Charlotte Shanks (1957-72), the second time to Sue Oran (1977-1992). Both of these marriages ended in divorce.

He is survived by third wife Julie Tokashiki, whom he married in 1998; sons Andy and Matt, a director, and daughter Erin by Shanks; and son Colin by Oran.

【次回のＥテレ・日曜美術館】

＜朝＞

奈良国立博物館で開催中の正倉院展。1300年以上、守り継がれた宝物9000件。その中から、初出陳11件を含む60件が展示されます。聖武天皇遺愛の品、当時一級の工芸品から日用品まで、多彩な宝物は厳重に管理され、継承されてきました。シルクロードを越えた東西の文化交流が結実した、「白瑠璃瓶」「漆胡瓶」、東大寺の大仏開眼会で用いられた「密陀彩絵箱」、謎のミイラ「虹龍」など、宝物に秘められた物語を紹介します。

司会: 坂本美雨,守本奈実 出演: 東儀秀樹,井上洋一

◇あわせて読みたい

＜夜＞

今年開創700年を迎える大徳寺。通常非公開の名宝の数々が東京国立博物館に集結しています。東洋絵画の最高峰といわれる国宝「観音猿鶴図」に表された“見えない音の世界”とは？一休宗純の気迫の墨 蹟 「七仏通戒偈」を書道家の武田双雲さんが分析します。そのほか、現代の妖怪漫画にも影響を与えた「百鬼夜行絵巻」や、奇跡の茶碗「曜変天目」など、大徳寺の至宝を堪能します。

article_text:
Films and events

Love

Coward

Lukas Dhont’s latest gem is a luminous and deeply romantic love story, set against the backdrop of the First World War.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director Lukas Dhont

Screenwriters Lukas Dhont, Angelo Tijssens

With Emmanuel Macchia, Valentin Campagne

Belgium-France-Netherlands 2026. 127min

Courtesy of MUBI

Languages French, Dutch With English subtitles

Certificate LFF18

Access information

Thursday 15 October 20:30

Descriptive subtitles

Sunday 18 October 15:25

Audio description

Descriptive subtitles

Find out about booking access tickets

Introduction

Quiet young farmer Pierre arrives on the battlefield to discover the horror of trench warfare. His ray of light is a cabaret run by the alluring Francis, who brings life, songs and the unexpected possibility of passionate love. Propelled by magnetic performances and enchanting musical acts, Coward demonstrates how art and desire illuminate dark and brutal times.

Laure Bonville

Content advice

Contains scenes of graphic violence or injury and nudity.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

Rose

Sandra Hüller gives an award-winning performance as a 17th-century female soldier who disguises herself as a man to gain acceptance in a brutal farming community.

A Man of His Time

The banality of evil is brilliantly exposed in this thought-provoking and singular portrait of a mediocre yet ambitious bureaucrat in Nazi-occupied France.

Frank and Percy

Roger Allam and Ian McKellen excel as the titular characters in this adaptation of the West End hit, about finding connection beyond your sixties.

article_text:
A Virginia man allegedly beheaded one of six statues at the Iwo Jima monument near the Quantico Marine base, causing what police estimated was hundreds of thousands of dollars in damage.

According to the incident report, Prince William County police arrived at the site Wednesday night to find 27-year-old Miguel Alonso Maldonado Soriano “actively damaging the statue with a sledgehammer.” The attack cost one of the monument’s Marines his head and left a second figure’s helmet and face “chipped and gouged.” The stone bayonet from the rifle carved over the back of a third statue was also missing.

Maldonado Soriano, 27, of Stafford, was arrested and faces two felony charges, injury to a monument and destruction of property and a misdemeanor charge of trespass with intent to damage property. A representative for the attorney assigned to Maldonado Soriano’s case declined to comment at the time of writing. He is being held without bond pending a court appearance.

The vandalized monument is a smaller version of Arlington’s Marine Corps War Memorial, which depicts a scene captured in a Pulitzer Prize-winning photograph by Joe Rosenthal of the Associated Press: Six US Marines raise the US flag atop Mount Suribachi on the Japanese island of Iwo Jima during World War II. (Rosenthal actually captured the second flag raising on the mountaintop, and for decades he was accused of staging the scene, an accusation he denied until his death.)

The US and Japanese militaries fought fiercely for control of the tactically valuable island, which, if taken, would mark the first Japanese home territory captured by the Americans. Of the six Marines in the photograph, only three survived the war. Three were killed within weeks of the photograph, before the battle for the mountaintop officially ended.

article_text:
I n films, twins are usually written as either identical personalities or complete and total opposites, and it’s the latter dynamic that’s at work in this pre-teen animation. One twin is a popular straight-A student heavily invested in fitting in and doing well at ballet, while her sister Mia is a chaotic kook. They both live in Primrose, an appropriately named community that apparently used to be infested with monsters, but can now claim to be proudly monster-free for the last 500 years. The twins’ parents are supportive of their golden child and try their best to understand Mia too, but it is easier for them to praise the kid bringing home the perfect behaviour reports than the one exasperating her teachers with her determination to discover monsters, by hook or by crook.

Scrappy Mia is, naturally, the protagonist of this film, and it’s not too long before she finds herself accidentally enrolled in Rotwood Academy, a school for monsters who would be shocked to discover a human in their midst; from their point of view, humans are brutal, cold-blooded creatures, best avoided, who prefer – ugh! – cupcakes to grave-worms. Mia quickly buddies up with some misfits including a vegan vampire, and the stage is thus set for some Addams Family Lite hijinks, with culture clash comedy highlighting the difference between monster norms and human ways providing much of the humour.

The underlying message that we shouldn’t be scared of difference is swiftly established as the major moral theme and while this is not exactly totally original, it proves distinctive enough to entertain its target audience. The message might be hammered home with all the subtlety of a croquet mallet to the head, but – what the hell – it is at least a wholesome philosophy, wrapped in palatable packaging. The Halloween timing of the release should help it connect enjoyably enough with younger spooky-season thrill-seekers.

White Cube Hong Kong 50 Connaught Road, Central Hong Kong +852 2592 2000 Tuesday – Saturday, 11am – 7pm

whitecube.com

The figurative paintings of Ethiopian-born artist Tesfaye Urgessa suspend compressed and fragmented bodies within spaces that resist ordinary logic, drawing the viewer into oneiric scenarios in which distinctions of place and time appear to fold into one another. Bringing together the artist’s most recent paintings, drawings and watercolours, The Lingering Departure extends this indeterminacy into matters of movement and migration, taking the apparent contradiction between ‘lingering’ and ‘departure’ to evoke the liminality of transit. Having spent over a decade moving between Addis Ababa and Germany, Urgessa regards departure as an ongoing condition: one that begins, as he describes it, in the anticipation of where one is going and persists through the memory of a place left behind.

Producer Will Packer has never been shy about sharing his opinion, even as he’s become a public figure. In a season when so many of Hollywood’s boldface names have kept a low profile when it comes to politics, Packer has taken to stages in recent weeks to advocate for causes and candidates that he believes in.

On Oct. 23, Packer led a rally at his alma mater, Florida A&M University in Tallahassee, where he urged students to flex their power by voting in Tuesday’s midterm elections. He appeared with Angie Nixon and David Jolly, Democratic candidates in Florida’s election for U.S. and governor, respectively. He told the crowd that decades of Republican control in the Sunshine State have led to significant underfunding of Florida A&M (also known as FAMU), and that it is time for change.

At the event, Packer revealed that he is launching a private fundraising effort for FAMU, which is part of Florida’s state university system. It is one of 107 schools in the U.S. that are designated Historically Black Colleges and Universities. Packer aims to build a private fundraising model for FAMU that he intends to extend to other HBCUs down the road.

Packer has built his public profile as a prolific supplier of distinctive movies and TV shows, from “Girls Trip” and “Straight Outta Compton” to the Peacock limited series “Fight Night” and the 2022 Academy Awards telecast. With the extraordinary events of the past two years — from the Trump administration’s assault on DEI programs to Florida’s efforts to denude the history of slavery from high school curriculums — Packer felt strongly motivated to speak out in support of candidates including Nixon and Jolly as well as Keisha Lance Bottoms, a Democrat who is running for governor of Georgia.

“I’m in a unique position because I work in Hollywood. I’m not in front of the camera, but I still have a profile, certainly with African American audiences who have been very supportive of my content,” Packer tells Variety . “I have always said that my opinion is not any more important than anybody else’s, but it’s certainly not any less important.”

Yes, taking strong position at a time of bitter political polarization in the U.S. is risky for any public figure. Packer feels a responsibility to speak out against what he sees as grave threats to the future of the nation and the democratic system. Packer echoes the sentiments of other commentators and pollsters who say a strong turnout among Black voters in key states such as Florida, Georgia and Texas could tip the scales for Democrats in those states.

“Turnout is the key to electoral success, and turnout is about energy and excitement. Black voters have been the key to the Democrats’ success because of our engaged turnout. When we are excited, engaged, and come out as a community and let our voices be heard, it matters,” Packer says. “So, for me, as somebody that’s got a very strong relationship with that community, I feel like I would be remiss if I wasn’t at least saying to people, ‘Let me tell you what I’m going to do. Let me tell you how I see this.’ ”

From Packer’s perspective, a large percentage of Black voters feel disenfranchised by the events of the past two years. He’s trying to remind them that the most powerful step they can take to initiate change is to fill out a ballot by Nov. 3.

“I see there’s an opportunity in places like the governorship in Georgia, the governorship in Florida, the Senate race in both states that I’m very close to and states where I know that Black voter turnout is absolutely going to matter,” Packer says. “I feel that it is incumbent upon me as somebody is never shy about saying, ‘Hey, you know what? This is what’s important in the movie industry. I think people should come out and support this type of film because this will say that to the industry that this is we should use our economic power.’ So why would I stop there, especially when it’s something that is so important? I think we’re in an existential moment in terms of our democracy and which direction we’re going to go.”

Packer’s FAMU rally was carried live on “Roland Martin Unfiltered,” the daily news and commentary program that airs on Martin’s Black Star Network and YouTube. “Roland Martin Unfiltered” has been on the road for the past two weeks, going deep into battleground states to cover local rallies and events and hosting lengthy discussions with local candidates well down the ballot.

Packer knows that there is considerable risk in being vocal about politics. He likens it to the dynamic that he encountered while trying to recruit a host for the 2022 Oscar telecast.

“I have a lot of friends across the industry who say that speaking out makes them very nervous because it’s so polarized. I was having a conversation with a very high-profile rapper-slash-actor. And this person said to me that there is literally no win to coming out and saying anything politically. You’re always going to piss off half the people, and especially right now, half the people are going to hate you if you say anything political at all. And that was this person’s very, very strong belief,” Packer says.

“It reminds me of when I was when I was having conversation with people about hosting the Oscars, and people said to me, ‘Why would I do this? I can only lose.’ So I hear the same thing about politics. But I feel like, we’re on this earth for however long God allows us to be. What are you doing with yourself and your human voice and your mission? If you’re not out there influencing people and doing things that you can feel proud of and sleep well at night, then have you really given it your all? Have you really made the most impactful legacy that you have on this earth? That’s why I got to where I am today,” he says.

Packer broke the news of his plan to launch the Rattler Freedom Fund (a nod to FAMU’s rattlesnake mascot) during the Oct. 23 rally. Since then, he’s received calls from other HBCUs looking to be involved. FAMU in recent years has been buffeted by “some very hard core MAGA philosophy” that has penetrated the Florida statehouse, he says.

“Florida A&M, like many HBCUs, is a public university, and so it is subject to the political leanings of whoever is in charge and in power. What we saw recently was something that many of us in the HBCU community thought could never happen, which is basically a MAGA takeover of a very, very prominent institution,” Packer says. “What we need to have is an independent financing source. This is not about Democrats versus Republicans. It is about HBCUs and saying we need to be able to fund our own purposes and aims and goals, independent of whoever may be in the governor’s house and whoever may control the state legislature. When you are completely dependent on resources and financing from a government, then you are subject to the whims of that government and we’re seeing that play out in real time.”

The fate of FAMU is deeply personal to Packer, who graduated magna cum laude in 1996 with a degree in electrical engineering. His career path was destined to take him to work the awards circuit more than circuit boards. But he credits the boost that he got from attending FAMU as providing the educational and cultural foundation that allowed him to take the radical detour to become a successful movie and TV producer.

“If it was not for my HBCU experience, I wouldn’t be where I am. It’s where I found my voice. This is something that we have to do in order to maintain these great, great institutions, who have who have helped create some of the greatest Black leaders and Black minds across so many fields. We have to create a system for us to be self-supporting and self-sustaining.”

Like all of Ferrara’s films, “Nine Lives” shows a vision that belies its disreputable roots — it stands alongside Wes Craven’s “The Fireworks Woman” and Radley Metzger’s “The Opening of Misty Beethoven” as one of the few genuine works of art in its genre."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RP_B2597.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "Julia Loktev at IndieWire Art of the Doc 2026 held at Lumen on October 19, 2026 in Los Angeles, California.", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/wildwood.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "Wildwood", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ferrara and Delia followed “Nine Lives” with another down-and-dirty, non-union indie exploitation film, the 1979 slasher opus “The Driller Killer.” A movie about a struggling artist (played by Ferrara under a pseudonym) who goes insane under the stress of failing to sell his work and pay his bills and resorts to murder as a result, “The Driller Killer” felt more than a little autobiographical, a violent howl of anguish and rage whose low budget and technical rough edges only made it more powerful."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“ Ms. 45 ” was ultimately made in reaction to those rough edges, after Ferrara was upset to overhear the distributor of “The Driller Killer” say the film didn’t look professional. “If anybody told me that now, I’d say, ‘Fuck you, it looks and sounds exactly the way it should,'” Ferrara told IndieWire. “But that attacked my ego in such a way that I said, ‘Fuck this. We’re gonna get rid of half the people we’re working with, we’re gonna get 35mm equipment, and we’re gonna do what everybody else does.”", "links": [{"text": "Ms. 45", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/ms-45/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ferrara now seems to have some regrets about not sticking to his guns and continuing to make underground, guerrilla films — “We were turning our backs on something that maybe we shouldn’t have turned our backs on,” he said — but the newfound polish he applied to “Ms. 45” is a large part of its impact. The core story, of a mute seamstress who becomes a vigilante after she’s assaulted by two different men in the same day, is reminiscent of “Death Wish” and all its grindhouse ripoffs, but the film stands alone thanks to the beauty of Ferrara’s visual style, the authentic feminist rage of Zoë Lund’s all-time great lead performance, and Delia’s propulsive, haunting score."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Delia knew then that he and Ferrara were moving to another level, partly thanks to new technology they could employ. “The VCR came into being right at the same time that we were starting to work on that score,” Delia told IndieWire. “On the first film, we had no picture to work with. On ‘Driller Killer,’ we sat at the Steenbeck and were scoring to picture, but we were loading up 35mm mag strips. Suddenly, on ‘Ms. 45,’ we had the ability to put the film up and go back and forth and not have to deal with any of that.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/MMDMSFO_EC001.jpg?w=650", "alt": "MS. 45, (aka MS. .45, aka MS 45), Zoe Tamerlis, 1981. ©Rochelle Films/Courtesy Everett Collection", "caption": "‘Ms. 45’ Everett Collection / Everett Collection", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The result was Delia’s first truly great score of many for Ferrara (they would go on to collaborate on “King of New York,” “Bad Lieutenant,” and about a dozen other fantastic movies). Delia credits the film’s strengths not only to the fact that he and Ferrara were able to work more efficiently with the VCR (the arrival of which Ferrara describes as being “like the invention of the printing press”), but also to the fact that they had top-notch collaborators that came from Ferrara’s desire to prove that he and his partners could make a professional-looking and sounding film."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“We had [engineer and producer] Larry Alexander, who did all the early Springsteen records,” Delia said. article_text:
45 years ago, director Abel Ferrara and composer Joe Delia collaborated on their third film together and made a classic: the exhilarating fusion of visual poetry, grindhouse violence, and poignant character study that was “ Ms. 45 .” On Thursday, Delia will perform his score live during a screening of the movie at the Southampton Playhouse , and then participate in a Q&A to discuss his work and his decades-long partnership with Ferrara.

The collaboration began with a mob-financed porno flick called “Nine Lives of a Wet Pussy,” a movie that nearly got Ferrara killed when it ran over schedule and budget (for hilarious stories about its making, check out Ferrara’s fantastic memoir, “Scene”). Like all of Ferrara’s films, “Nine Lives” shows a vision that belies its disreputable roots — it stands alongside Wes Craven’s “The Fireworks Woman” and Radley Metzger’s “The Opening of Misty Beethoven” as one of the few genuine works of art in its genre.

Ferrara and Delia followed “Nine Lives” with another down-and-dirty, non-union indie exploitation film, the 1979 slasher opus “The Driller Killer.” A movie about a struggling artist (played by Ferrara under a pseudonym) who goes insane under the stress of failing to sell his work and pay his bills and resorts to murder as a result, “The Driller Killer” felt more than a little autobiographical, a violent howl of anguish and rage whose low budget and technical rough edges only made it more powerful.

“ Ms. 45 ” was ultimately made in reaction to those rough edges, after Ferrara was upset to overhear the distributor of “The Driller Killer” say the film didn’t look professional. “If anybody told me that now, I’d say, ‘Fuck you, it looks and sounds exactly the way it should,'” Ferrara told IndieWire. “But that attacked my ego in such a way that I said, ‘Fuck this. We’re gonna get rid of half the people we’re working with, we’re gonna get 35mm equipment, and we’re gonna do what everybody else does.”

Ferrara now seems to have some regrets about not sticking to his guns and continuing to make underground, guerrilla films — “We were turning our backs on something that maybe we shouldn’t have turned our backs on,” he said — but the newfound polish he applied to “Ms. 45” is a large part of its impact. The core story, of a mute seamstress who becomes a vigilante after she’s assaulted by two different men in the same day, is reminiscent of “Death Wish” and all its grindhouse ripoffs, but the film stands alone thanks to the beauty of Ferrara’s visual style, the authentic feminist rage of Zoë Lund’s all-time great lead performance, and Delia’s propulsive, haunting score.

Delia knew then that he and Ferrara were moving to another level, partly thanks to new technology they could employ. “The VCR came into being right at the same time that we were starting to work on that score,” Delia told IndieWire. “On the first film, we had no picture to work with. On ‘Driller Killer,’ we sat at the Steenbeck and were scoring to picture, but we were loading up 35mm mag strips. Suddenly, on ‘Ms. 45,’ we had the ability to put the film up and go back and forth and not have to deal with any of that.”

The result was Delia’s first truly great score of many for Ferrara (they would go on to collaborate on “King of New York,” “Bad Lieutenant,” and about a dozen other fantastic movies). Delia credits the film’s strengths not only to the fact that he and Ferrara were able to work more efficiently with the VCR (the arrival of which Ferrara describes as being “like the invention of the printing press”), but also to the fact that they had top-notch collaborators that came from Ferrara’s desire to prove that he and his partners could make a professional-looking and sounding film.

“We had [engineer and producer] Larry Alexander, who did all the early Springsteen records,” Delia said. Although “Ms. 45” was a low-budget film compared to studio thrillers of the time like “Marathon Man,” Ferrara’s determination and ability to call in favors made it feel almost equally well-resourced. “We had connections, so we reached out and got a union crew. We did the sound mix where Woody Allen did his mixes,” Ferrara said. “We had top-of-the-line studio musicians, and the same equipment the Beatles did ‘Sgt. Pepper’ with, you dig? Everything we had was state of the art.”

Ferrara’s ingenuity in piggybacking on larger productions even landed him his lead actress, whom Ferrara and Delia both credit with making “Ms. 45” the classic it has become. “Robert Stigwood was going to produce a movie called ’42nd Street’ after ‘Saturday Night Fever,'” Ferrara said. “They thought this was gonna be the greatest movie in the world.” Stigwood launched a highly publicized worldwide talent search to find his lead, echoing what David O. Selznick did when he made “Gone With the Wind.”

Lund was one of the thousands of actresses who auditioned. “These friends of mine were part of the casting, and they were basically doing a million-dollar casting search,” Ferrara said. “I called them up, and they said, ‘We got your girl, bro. They’re never gonna use her. We can’t give you her name now, we’ve got to wait for them to cast who they want, but wait until you see this chick.'” Once Lund was no longer a factor on the Stigwood project, Ferrara’s friends sent her to his office.

“She steps off the elevator, and the first second I saw her, I said, ‘Fuck yeah,'” Ferrara said. “I don’t care what she says, I don’t care how crazy she is.” Ferrara had his leading lady, and they would go on to co-write “Bad Lieutenant” together before Lund’s tragic death at 37 from heart failure related to her drug addiction. “She was a genius. She knew more than anyone about anything, any subject. What a find she was. She was exceptional at 17, she was still brilliant in her 30s even though she was junked out of her mind. What a fucking tragedy.”

Ferrara said Lund immediately understood the power and subtext of Nicholas St. John’s script, which arrived on Ferrara’s doorstep like a gift. “When Nicky wrote it, he didn’t talk about it,” Ferrara said. “He was superstitious. This was not a script that everyone worked on and gave notes on. It just arrived, and I read it and thought, ‘How the fuck does this cat do this?’ Because he was our bro. All I had to do was take it to the screen.”

Just as Ferrara knew what he had when he read St. John’s script, Delia knew what they had when he saw the first screening of the movie. “I had delivered all the music, and wasn’t around all that much for the mix,” Delia said. “I sat in that theater, and it was turned up loud, and it just sounded so fucking good. And the casting of Zoë…she was just a miraculous find.” Revisiting the film to prepare the live score, Delia was “knocked out all over again.”

For the live performance at the Southampton Playhouse, Delia plans to recreate the score with a few new twists, bringing in some additional musicians along with a rig of computers and samples from the original film. For all of the advanced technology he and Ferrara had when they stepped up from the underground of “Driller Killer” to go mainstream with “Ms. 45,” the filmmakers recall that they still went for some lo-fi approaches to the music and sound back when they made the film.

“Even with all these brilliant musicians and the four-track, we still used this sound effects record,” Ferrara said. “It was probably made in the 1960s. And it had this thing called ‘Monster Approaching.’ We must have used that on five movies, and it’s all over ‘Ms. 45.'” “It’s just a sting, something we could easily do electronically now,” Delia said. “But it was so perfect.”

Ferrara also came up with a simple but effective way of getting the best sound effect that he could for a gunshot. “There’s a moment in ‘Apocalypse Now’ with the scariest, perfect gunshot,” Ferrara said. After a sound mixer told Ferrara the story of how Coppola spent $50,000 and finally got the gunshot sound he wanted, Ferrara had an idea. “I told the sound guy, ‘Listen man, go see ‘Apocalypse Now’ in the middle of the afternoon when nobody’s there and wait for that moment. Record that .45.’ That gunshot cost $50,000 and we got it for nothing, because they’re never going to be able to track it.”

Years after the movie came out, Ferrara and Delia got the ultimate compliment when they learned that David Bowie had named “Ms. 45” one of the greatest film scores of all time. “David Bowie wrote down his 10 favorite scores, and this guy was a cineaste,” Ferrara said. “He saw everything. And ‘Ms. 45’ is on that list of 10.” When Delia saw his score was number three, he called Ferrara.

“I said, ‘Did you see this?’ And Abel said, ‘Yeah, that’s your fucking diploma. Hang it on the wall.'”

“Ms. 45” will screen at the Southampton Playhouse on October 22 with a live score and Q&A.

article_text:
Indian filmmakers Anurag Kashyap and Vasan Bala have come on board to present “ Aakhri Ride ,” a short thriller set over a single Halloween night in Mumbai, which will release worldwide on Oct. 31.

The film will go out on Oh Short Flips, a YouTube channel curated by Kashyap.

Vijesh Rajan and Yashoda Parthasarthy wrote and directed the short, their first film. It follows a Mumbai ride-share driver who is driven to breaking point during one frightening night.

Kashyap said he had worked with the pair since the “Gangs of Wasseypur” days and “always believed they are excellent storytellers with a unique visual language. So when they finally decided to turn writer-directors, it was an easy decision to back them. And now, I am quite excited to see the audience’s response to their first film – ‘Aakhri Ride,’ when it releases on Halloween Day.”

Chandan Roy (“Panchayat”) and Aamir Dalvi (“Kennedy”) head the cast, and Faisal Malik (“Panchayat”) also appears. Ranjan Singh, Vishesh Agrawal, Rajan EPK and Kashyap produced, with Navaras Pictures backing the project in association with Plexus Motion Pictures and Flip Films.

Bala described Rajan as the “Wiz Kid” that filmmaker Srinivas had introduced him and his colleagues to. “We were always in awe of what he could do with his VFX skills but there was always a sensitive and fun storyteller in him. When he and Yashoda went to make the film, we all rooted for them. I was beyond excited to watch their short film. It’s sharp, fun, quirky and with a beating heart. So coming on board was a nano second decision, a no brainer,” Bala said.

The directors traced the idea back to long taxi rides home after meetings around the city. “We’d be sitting in the back seat, talking about work or sitting in silence, while the driver was often carrying a completely different world on his phone: family back home, money worries, things we may never fully know. We began to notice an invisible social divide: we were enjoying the comfort of being driven home, while he was trying to make ends meet. We shared a small space, but knew so little about each other’s lives,” they said.

The pair set out to examine that gap through a mix of horror and comedy, built around a man so weighed down by daily problems that he fails to see what he has picked up. “We hope viewers laugh, get spooked, and maybe think a little about the person driving them home,” they said.

The film began its festival run in the Short Film Market Picks at Clermont-Ferrand , then landed selections at three genre events: BIFAN in Bucheon, Fantasia International Film Festival and Fantastic Fest. Its circuit, which includes Oscar- and BAFTA-qualifying festivals, also took in Florida Film Festival, Austin After Dark, Wench, Fantaspoa, events in Rhode Island and San Jose, Italy’s Absurd Film Festival, France’s Red Movie Awards, Cannes Indie Shorts and New York Indie Shorts Awards.

At Fantasia, the short won the Silver Audience Award for best Asian short. It also picked up best film at the Dada Saheb Phalke Film Festival and best Indian short at the Indo Dubai International Film Festival, and finished as second runner-up at BISFF.

article_text:
Jennifer Lawrence has officially entered the celebrity beauty game with the launch of her haircare brand Mes, but the Oscar winner’s career pivot is not a reaction to Hollywood instability. Speaking to The Cut , Lawrence said that if she worried about the money Hollywood could bring in then “a smarter exit plan would be signing up for a big franchise.”

“Starting a new company to get rich feels like jumping off a cruise ship to land on a door,” the actor added.

‘Wildwood’ Director Travis Knight on AI: 'An Amazing Piece of Technology’ but ‘I’m Not Embracing It at All’

Mes, per The Cut, is a “biodesigned haircare” company that is “selling three products: a repair mask, a restyling serum, and a volumizing mist. [Lawrence] partnered with an MIT-trained scientist to develop new formulas they claim will change your hair in ways nothing else on the market can.”

Lawrence explained that moving from acting into the haircare space felt like a natural extension of her interests as a performer because “there is an undeniable energetic thing that happens when you’re creating things, whether it’s a movie or a product. I got that same electric buzz I get from building a character. It’s like, ‘Well, I have to follow this because it’s the same animal.'”

So what is Lawrence most nervous about as she launches a beauty brand? She told The Cut she hopes people stick with the products and don’t grow impatient.

“If you make a texturizing spray, everybody knows what to expect,” Lawrence explained. “These are brand-new products. So my fear is somebody will get a first impression without actually taking the time to figure out how it works with their hair.”

Lawrence added of waiting to see the reception, “I imagine it’s going to be like when a movie comes out, where there has to be this release of tension. I’ll try and get Zen with it. But I’ll probably just have wine for breakfast.”

Aaron Guzikowski , creator of the Scott Free -produced HBO Max sci-fi series Raised by Wolves , is scripting a new Alien movie for 20th Century Studios , Deadline can confirm.

An American screenwriter and showrunner, Guzikowski’s Raised by Wolves — following two androids raising human children following the destruction of the Earth in a great war — aired for two seasons. He’s otherwise best known for penning Prisoners , Warner Bros.’ lauded 2013 crime thriller directed by Denis Villeneuve.

article_text:
Joel McHale ’s next move could be a viral sensation.

McHale is set to star in the next short film from director Kevin Cate , the pair confirmed in a collaborative video on Oct. 23. No information outside of McHale’s casting is known about the short film, but Cate is set to collaborate again with the same core team that made “ Open Door ,” “Birthday Flight” and “Unbearable Christmas” under his Clinging Vine Films banner.

Related Stories

Inde Navarrette Wins Halloween With Penis-Destroying Robot ‘SNL’ Sketch ‘The Inventor’s Wife’

'SNL' Sets Druski as First Online Content Creator to Host

Cate’s 2023 sci-fi short “Open Door” received over 33 million views across YouTube shorts, TikTok and Instagram, and is going to be adapted into a feature .

Cate has also been busy directing his first feature, “Unbearable Christmas,” starring Julia Stiles, Alex Moffat, David Cross and Stephen Root. He also released his latest short film, “ Birthday Flight ,” in Sept. That work, which follows a man who dozes off on a plane and wakes up to find it empty, has hit a million views on various platforms.

McHale is best known as a host and comedic ringer on scores of shows, known for his acerbic wit on current series like “The 1% Club,” “House of Villains” and “Crime Scene Kitchen.” He also stars on the Fox sitcom “Animal Control,” which is now in its fifth season. Previously, he hosted the cult favorite clip show “The Soup” and was the star of the gone-too-soon sitcom “Community.”

In film, McHale appeared this year in “Scream 7” and the satire “Stop! That! Train!” He’s also had roles in “Spider-Man 2,” “Ted,” “Becky” and “Blended.”

article_text:
W hen Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo – the directing duo known in their native Spain as “Los Javis” – began writing their queer epic La Bola Negra, they weren’t thinking about whether it would be stylish (which it is) or win numerous awards (which it has) or capture what they refer to as “the anti-fascist zeitgeist” (which it does). Instead, they thought only of scale. “I’m done with LGBTQ+ movies being niche,” says Ambrossi. “I was like, ‘Let’s make the biggest, gayest war movie ever .’” Job done.

At Cannes this year, the best director prize was awarded jointly to them and to Paweł Pawlikowski, who made the Thomas Mann road trip film Fatherland . La Bola Negra is now an Oscars frontrunner, with best picture and best director nominations all but guaranteed. Brimming with panache, the movie darts back and forth between three stories set in Spain: in 1932, a young man applying for membership of an exclusive casino is rejected on the grounds of his suspected homosexuality; in 1937, a callow nationalist soldier develops tender feelings for the injured republican prisoner under his watch; and in 2017, a queer historian inherits an unfinished story by Federico García Lorca. That story lends the movie its title and provides the thread that sews its strands together.

Throw in spectacular set pieces, Ken Russell-style visual flair, cameos from a blond-wigged Penélope Cruz and a Spanish-speaking Glenn Close, and the result is a maximalist collage where the Spanish civil war sits side-by-side with Grindr hook-ups. “We loved imagining scenes that you don’t usually have in queer movies,” says Ambrossi, citing the spectacular opening sequence in which a Spanish village is bombed by Italian fascists. “A lot of people have said they’ve been missing something like this. They want to buy popcorn and be given a big movie like Titanic.” His eyes widen. “This is the gay Titanic!”

Relaxing at a corner table in the restaurant of a London hotel, Los Javis represent a study in contrasts. Ambrossi is 42, dinky and loquacious, his impish face crowned with a laurel of curls. He leans forward as he talks, arms folded on the white tablecloth. The taller, taciturn Calvo, 35, is gravely handsome. Battling jet lag, he repeatedly stretches his limbs like a cat, sneaking a glance at himself in the mirror next to the table as he does so. Both men have black caterpillar eyebrows, as well as cheekbones that could double as clothing rails.

On this chilly autumn morning, Los Javis could do with some extra layers. They rub their bare arms furiously until an assistant arrives bearing hoodies. Then again, maybe the three of us have goosebumps not from the cold but from discussing their film. Ambrossi approves of this theory: “There’s a trend on TikTok where people video themselves – ‘This is us before watching La Bola Negra’ – and then it cuts to afterwards when they’re crying and hugging. All this togetherness from the cinematic experience is beautiful.” No wonder Los Javis insisted on an extended theatrical window for their film before selling the US rights to Netflix. La Bola Negra will remain in US cinemas for 47 days, a record for the streaming platform. Even Scorsese didn’t get that.

The movie also marks a personal breakthrough for the pair, who first met when they were actors. “Friends who read the script said to us, ‘Oh, you’re going there? ’” recalls Ambrossi. “We’ve been writing together for 13 years about LGBTQ+ characters but it has always been, like, lesbians, trans women …” Previous collaborations include their 2017 debut film, Holy Camp!, which they adapted from La Llamada, their stage musical about a summer camp staffed by nuns. In one scene, God materialises to sing I Will Always Love You. Their 2023 series La Mesías (now streaming on Mubi ) is a hypnotically bizarre tale of Christian pop stars, extraterrestrials and bad parenting. But no gay men.

What took them so long? “Sometimes you don’t want to talk about yourself,” offers Calvo, speaking up at last. “Many queer creators have projected themselves into other characters. Pedro Almodóvar, Lorca with The House of Bernarda Alba, Michael Patrick King with Sex and the City.” He flashes a rare smile. “Good show.”

Ambrossi identifies a psychological dimension to the delay: “It’s true you don’t want to be too on-the-nose. But you start wondering if there is also another reason.” In the 1932 strand of the film, the elite casino members use a system of black and white balls to vote on admitting newcomers. The black ball for no– la bola negra – becomes a symbol of queer generational shame and rejection that must be wrestled with. Is it shame, then, that kept Ambrossi from addressing his own sexuality in his work? “In my case, yes. I wasn’t ready to talk about desire or sex because I felt ashamed in some way.”

He and Calvo were already friends with their compatriot and hero Almodóvar, whose company El Deseo, meaning Desire, co-produced La Bola Negra. “I told Pedro, ‘I don’t deal well with desire.’ He looked at me and said, ‘You need to start.’ That’s when it clicked: if you don’t deal explicitly with desire, you are missing life.”

Perhaps that is why the word “explicit” crops up several times in Ambrossi’s conversation today: having been out as a gay man but under the radar in his work, he is eager now to emphasise the ways in which La Bola Negra is defiant or unequivocal. One aspect is the casting of gay actors in gay roles, most notably the Bambi-eyed singer Guitarricadelafuente, who makes his screen debut as the lovestruck soldier.

“It’s not that straight actors can’t play gay,” says Calvo. “There are no rules in art. But …” Ambrossi jumps in: “We like to do it this way. When I was 10, I watched Rupert Everett in My Best Friend’s Wedding. I wasn’t sure I was gay, but I knew he was like me. There was a truth in his eyes that I want to get in my movies.” He sighs. “Rupert Everett was so brave. He should have been James Bond.”

Calvo had an unhappy experience as a young gay actor. “I was a teenager playing a gay role on TV,” he says. “When it finished, I didn’t get many auditions. I was advised to cut my hair, not paint my nails.” A short back and sides didn’t help, though. “I guess people could still tell. So I decided to write roles for actors who don’t have space in the industry.”

Once the pair began dating as well as working together, the two-headed queer celebrity phenomenon of Los Javis was born. They were playwrights, film-makers, actors and reality TV participants, including regular judges on the Spanish version of Ru Paul’s Drag Race. Being an indispensable part of Spanish cultural life came at a price. Calvo points to this now as one of the reasons he and Ambrossi separated during the making of La Bola Negra. “People would talk to me in the plural all the time, ‘It was nice to meet you guys.’ I’d be like, ‘Huh? I’m standing alone here.’ I felt I’d lost my individuality.”

Spain didn’t cope well with the breakup. “It was a big deal,” Calvo admits. “There were cameras outside my door for a month.” Keen to move on, Ambrossi displays a flicker of irritation: “I think we’ve passed through this conversation. Imagine everyone talking about your ex forever! We love to write and direct together and we’re going to keep doing that.” The matter is closed.

After all the diversifying and cross-platforming, Los Javis have reached their Pokémon-style final evolution. “From now on, we want to focus on movies,” says Calvo. No regrets, though. “The other things were important in making a statement,” Ambrossi points out. “I grew up thinking directors should be serious and monolithic. We represented a new way.” Calvo lifts a finger: “A non-binary way,” he says. “We don’t see life as stiff. We mix genres. A more flexible time is coming. Take the work seriously but not yourself.”

Before they go, there is a line in La Bola Negra that I ask them to unpack. When the modern-day researcher Alberto asks the Lorca scholar played by Glenn Close for advice on what he should do with the pages of that incomplete story, she tells him: “You’ve inherited something and you don’t know what to do with it. You are truly a Spaniard.”

Calvo is happy to help. “In Spain, we always have to be reminded by foreigners that we have a rich, interesting culture and history,” he says. Ambrossi elaborates: “It is as if pride is shameful. When someone is doing well and winning awards all over Spain, people are like, ‘Hmm. That’s not very Spanish.’ Unless it’s football.” Where does that attitude come from? “Maybe religion,” muses Calvo. “Maybe dictatorship.”

Does it apply to them? Are they destined to underplay their triumphs for ever? They offer their best you’ve-got-to-be-kidding looks, then answer in unison: “Not us.”

article_text:
Talent management and production company Fusion Entertainment has signed writer-director Ryan DeForeest and started development on a feature adaptation of his short film “My Brother & Me,” Variety can reveal exclusively.

“My Brother & Me,” which premiered at the 2024 American Black Film Festival, follows “two brothers across three decades, from South Los Angeles to Oakland, as they grow up under their father, Allen. Malik, the older one, takes the brunt of Allen’s violence. Terrence, who is gay, grows up feeling invisible to him. As they become men, the only thing they’ve ever really had is each other, and even that isn’t guaranteed,” reads the official description. Zechariah Eubanks and Alexander Bello starred as Malik and Terrence, respectively.

Related Stories

Sanjay Gupta, Indian Director of 'Kaante' and 'Zinda,' Dies at 59

Quentin Tarantino Confirms He's ‘Written a Script’ for His Tenth Film, But Won’t Pursue It Yet Because He Wants to ‘Live a Little’

“Ryan is a rare new voice whose filmmaking belongs right alongside our roster of distinctive auteurs with an unmistakable point of view,” said Chris Evans, co-founder of Fusion Entertainment. “This story speaks to the experience of Black fatherhood, masculinity, queerness, and the complicated, tender dynamics of brotherhood.”

“My Brother & Me” has since screened at Micheaux Film Festival, the Oak Park Black Film Festival and NewFilmmakers Los Angeles. It earned a nomination for outstanding short form (live action) at the 56th NAACP Image Awards, along with two 2026 Best of NFMLA Awards nominations for best short film (drama) and best cinematography.

“‘My Brother & Me’ started as a personal story made with some of my favorite people in the world,” said DeForeest. “Seeing the journey this short has taken and having the opportunity to expand it into my first feature is something I never could have imagined. I’m incredibly grateful to Chris and Adam for believing in the potential of this film and the many other stories I hope to tell. I’m so stoked to begin this next chapter with them and continue creating work that reflects the complexity and vulnerability of the communities I hold dear.”

Evans and Adam Kersh will produce for Fusion, alongside Lexx Truss, who produced “My Brother & Me” with Shandrea Evans. Returning from the short are cinematographer Sade Ndya and composer Evan Wright. The feature is currently in development. Casting and an updated title will be revealed at a future date.

article_text:
Daylight Books published Archive/Journal: 1985-1995/2001 by Vincent Cianni.

From 1985 to 1995, at the height of the AIDS epidemic, Vincent Cianni photographed New York City’s Pride marches from street level, up close and inside the crowd. His pictures hold celebration and grief together as one: a community gathering in public while it was losing thousands of its own.

Twenty-five years later, during the Covid-19 pandemic, Cianni returned to the negatives. He spent six to eight hours a day, five to six days a week in the darkroom, culling hundreds of rolls of film and thinking about what the two health crises shared.

The result is Archive/Journal: 1985-1995/2001 , a two-volume slipcased book published by Daylight Books in June 2026. One volume looks outward at the marches. The other looks inward at the life Cianni was living alongside them.

Volume 1: Archive 1985-1995

Archive 1985-1995 collects 80 black-and-white photographs made at the marches, along with ephemera, newspaper clippings, and timelines of the political, social, and cultural events around them. The marches were celebrations, and they were also protests. Marchers demanded an end to the stigma and criminalization of HIV, funding for treatment research, and legal, housing, and medical services for people who had no access to them.

Cianni’s epilogue acknowledges Marsha P. Johnson and Sylvia Rivera, shown marching side by side in the 1989 NYC Pride March twenty years after the Stonewall uprising, as pivotal figures in the Gay Liberation Movement.

New York writer Miss Rosen contributes an essay on the role Pride played inside the devastation of the epidemic. “Pride, always a political act, became a lifeline,” she writes, “a place where people came together as one in real space and time.”

Volume 2: Journal 1985-2001

Journal 1985-2001 turns to Cianni’s own life during those years. It pairs his journal entries with self-portraits and portraits of friends and lovers who were living with AIDS or died of it. The entries are intimate and unguarded, written as events unfolded.

Throughout the book are friends, lovers, and partners who sustained him, photographed in their homes, their beds, at birthday parties, in clubs, on the road, and in other domestic and public spaces. Cianni dedicates the book “for Jonathan, Scott, Matthew, Antonio, and those I loved, lost, and live on with.”

Returning to his epilogue, Cianni sets the AIDS years beside the pandemic he was living through as he printed, and beside the police violence and protests that followed the murder of George Floyd in 2020:

“Looking through these photographs, I realized how many of the same battles persist. Hatred, discrimination, and inadequate government responses remain hauntingly familiar. Yet the images also serve as a testament to the power of activism, resilience, and hope.”

article_text:
Elon Musk isn’t having much of a week. He spent hundreds of millions of dollars on the midterm elections, only to have his preferred Republican candidates lose. And now he’s taking it on the chin from Robert De Niro .

The Oscar-winning actor was joined by his fellow Tribeca Festival founder Jane Rosenthal for a screening in New York City Sunday of Musk , Alex Gibney ’s documentary that is highly critical of the world’s richest man. We understand a roomful of Academy members was on hand for the event at the Crosby Hotel in Manhattan.

“Elon Musk spent about 300 million dollars getting Trump elected in 2024,” De Niro said as he introduced the film. “And he just spent close to half a billion on Republicans in this past week’s election. How did that turn out for you?” he said to cheers and laughter.

De Niro alluded to more bad news for Musk this week – his announcement on X that Tesla would end production of the much-ballyhooed Cybertruck next summer.

“In the fight between Musk’s money and democracy, democracy won. This time. But just like his grotesque Cybertruck, Musk isn’t going anywhere,” De Niro commented. “It’s a reminder that while we are celebrating the massive electoral repudiation of Trump and Trumpism, we have to be vigilant — and not just vigilant, we have to be ready to take action. This is an important film, I hope you will be as moved as I was by it and spread the word.”

For his part, Oscar winner Gibney told De Niro, “Thank you, Bob, for all you have done for all of the resistance.”

Musk , with a running time of 3 hours 52 minutes, is now available on VOD platforms. Released theatrically by Bleecker Street, the documentary has made over $700,000 at the domestic box office.

“I admit I was apprehensive before watching this film, the first time I saw it. I mean four hours, Alex, really?” Rosenthal kidded Gibney. “Four hours in the company of Elon Musk — it is a lot to ask. It is a thoroughly engrossing film about a thoroughly gross character. A character we cannot ignore.”

Rosenthal added, “2,500 years ago, Sun Tzu [author of The Art of War ] cautioned us to know your enemy. Musk the film exposes Musk the man and we cannot look away.”

On Sunday night, Musk won Best Biographical Documentary at the Critics Choice Documentary Awards in New York. It premiered at the Venice Film Festival and went on to screen at the Toronto Film Festival, Camden International Film Festival, Zurich Film Festival, BFI London Film Festival and more. It screens later this week at DOC NYC after making that festival’s prestigious shortlist of the year’s best documentaries. Musk is also slated to screen this month at IDFA in Amsterdam, the world’s biggest documentary film festival.
